references.title: Quantifying electron-transfer in liquid-solid contact electrification and the formation of electric double-layer
references.authors: Shiquan Lin, Liang Xu, Aurelia Chi Wang, Zhong Lin Wang
references.actually_read: Abstract; introduction; visible results on DI-water/SiO2 charging and solution/pH dependence; discussion.
references.evidence: The authors experimentally distinguish removable electron-associated charge from more persistent ion-associated charge in selected liquid/ceramic contacts. Their reported carrier contributions depend on solution and surface conditions. The introduction also identifies electron, ion and material-transfer mechanisms proposed for different contact systems.
references.limits: Supports the possibility of non-electron contributions and condition dependence, not a universal mechanism, a comb/hair polarity prediction, or a solid-solid quantitative transfer law. The paper's universal-sounding introductory language and numerical experimental data are not imported. Output was truncated in other portions; no claim of a complete paper/supplement/figure review.

references.title: EOS/ESD Fundamentals Part 2: Principles of ESD Control
references.actually_read: Opening fundamentals summary; Basic Principles of Static Control, especially Reduce Electrostatic Charge Generation and Dissipate and Neutralize; control-program assessment and conclusion.
references.evidence: Conductors can be triboelectrically charged; transferred/retained charge depends on material, contact/separation and humidity. Conductive pathways and grounding can dissipate charge, whereas common insulators lack a sufficiently conductive pathway for ordinary grounding to remove charge promptly. Effective control requires assessment rather than reliance on one product or procedure.
references.limits: The association's own electronics-ESD guidance supports the physical mobility/retention distinction, not certification of any rubber glove, industrial ignition protection, or learner operating instructions. Standards/version/voltage recommendations are not adopted.

references.title: Combustible Dust: An Explosion Hazard - Overview
references.evidence: Finely divided combustible material suspended in air at an appropriate concentration can become explosible under suitable conditions. This supports distinguishing combustible dust from arbitrary dust and conditional risk from inevitable ignition.
references.limits: No incident statistics, legal requirements, ignition-energy number, material-specific guarantee or handling instructions imported. The lesson's adequate-ignition-energy condition is assessed as a necessary physical condition, not a quantitative threshold supplied by this overview.

reused.use: Retained elementary-charge context only; no refetch and no new numerical constant added to the lesson.
